title: Locus (coordinate)
examples: How do I find the locus if the point P is always equidistant from two points?
If I know the equation of the locus, can I find the original geometric condition?
What is the difference between finding a locus and finding the equation of a circle?

explain.say: Today we are learning about the locus of a point.
The locus is simply the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition.
For example, the locus of a point P that moves at a constant distance from a fixed point is a circle.
Let us find the locus of a point P that moves such that the sum of its distances from two fixed points is constant.

faq.q: What is the locus if the point P is always equidistant from two fixed points?
faq.a: The locus is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining those two fixed points.
asks: What line is equidistant from two points?
If I use the distance formula, what shape do I get?

faq.q: Do I always use the distance formula when finding a locus?
faq.a: The distance formula is very useful, but sometimes simplifying the initial geometric condition first is easier.
asks: Is there another way to calculate the distance?
When is the distance formula not the best method?

faq.q: If the locus is a straight line, what does that mean geometrically?
faq.a: It means the point P is restricted to moving only along that specific straight line.
asks: What does a linear locus look like?
Does a straight line count as a locus?

faq.q: What if the fixed points are the same point?
faq.a: If the two fixed points are the same, the locus is simply the circle centered at that point with a radius equal to the constant distance.
asks: What happens if the two points merge?
Is it always a circle if the points are the same?

faq.q: Can I use calculus to find the locus?
faq.a: While calculus can be used for optimization on a curve, the standard method for locus relies on algebraic manipulation of distance formulas.
asks: Is differentiation needed for this topic?

facts: The locus is the set of all points satisfying a given condition.
If the condition involves a constant sum of distances from two points, the locus is an ellipse.
If the condition involves a constant product of distances, the locus can be more complex.
The perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equidistant from two given points.

quiz.say: Find the locus of a point P(x, y) such that the distance from P to (1, 0) equals the distance from P to (-1, 0).
quiz.why: The condition means P is on the perpendicular bisector, which is the y-axis, so x equals zero.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it calculates the distance to just one point, not the equality between two distances.
wrong.2: This is wrong because it only uses the x-coordinate of one point, not the equality of distances.
wrong.3: This is wrong because it assumes the locus must lie on the x-axis, which is not guaranteed.

quiz.say: What is the locus of a point P(x, y) such that the sum of its distances from (2, 0) and (-2, 0) is 10?
quiz.why: This directly translates the geometric condition into an equation using the distance formula for both points.

wrong.0: This incorrectly squares the sum of the distances, mixing the terms together.
wrong.1: This assumes the locus is a circle centered at the origin, ignoring the two distinct foci.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake from misremembering the standard form of the ellipse equation.

quiz.say: The locus of a point P(x, y) such that the distance from P to (0, 0) is always 5 is:
quiz.why: This constant distance from the origin defines a circle with a radius of five units.

wrong.0: This incorrectly uses the constant distance as the radius squared, instead of squaring the constant.
wrong.1: This incorrectly doubles the required equation, perhaps by adding the distance to itself.
wrong.3: This equation represents a straight line, not a circle centered at the origin.
